artworks.title: Troilus and Cressida, Act 1
artworks.description: Kirk's Boydell Shakespeare Gallery plate stages Act 1 of Troilus and Cressida — Pandarus as go-between for the Trojan lovers, the Homeric archer rewritten as the comic bawd of English stage tradition.

artworks.title: Pandarus and Cressida
artworks.description: This Metropolitan Museum print of Troilus and Cressida Act 1 Scene 2 freezes Pandarus with Cressida — Shakespeare's middleman, far from the Iliad's Lycian archer who breaks the truce, yet still named for him.

films.title: Troy: Fall of a City
films.description: The BBC/Netflix Trojan War series restores Pandarus among the Trojan ranks — the archer of Book 4 whose broken truce the cycle still remembers.

popCulture.title: Iliad
popCulture.creator: Homer
popCulture.description: Iliad 4 makes Pandarus the Lycian archer who, urged by Athena, shoots Menelaus and shatters the truce — the wound that restarts the war.

popCulture.title: Troilus and Criseyde
popCulture.creator: Geoffrey Chaucer
popCulture.description: Chaucer's Pandarus is uncle and go-between for Troilus and Criseyde — the medieval rewrite that turned Homer's archer into English literature's archetype of the pander.

popCulture.title: Troilus and Cressida
popCulture.creator: William Shakespeare
popCulture.description: Shakespeare's bitter comedy keeps Pandarus as the bawd of Troy — the stage figure whose name English already treated as a synonym for a procurer.

popCulture.title: pander
popCulture.description: English 'pander' (noun and verb) derives from Pandarus' medieval role as go-between — a rare case of a Homeric name becoming ordinary moral vocabulary.
